# The slow fix

> A sentence is finished when nothing is left to take away.
> — an invented line, written only for the test

Every draft I have ever written started to look better the week I stopped reading it. That is a trick of distance, and it fools me every time. The page has not changed. My eyes have.

I began to keep a notebook of the things I do when I revise, and the list was humbling. I walk to the window. I make tea. I open the file and read the first paragraph three times, and then I close it again. All of a sudden the afternoon is gone, and the only thing I have fixed is the title.

My friend Anna says that revision is just reading with a pencil. I think she is right, but I would add that it is reading slowly, patiently, and without mercy. She revises quietly, carefully and almost invisibly, the way a tailor works. I revise loudly and badly. We both end up with a better text, which is the only measure that counts.

I use a few small checks, and none of them is clever. The first is the echo. If I use the word "window" in one line and again two lines later, the reader hears it twice, even when I did not mean it. A window, a window, a pane of glass: the repetition turns a plain word into a drumbeat. Echoes are easy to miss in your own prose because you know what you meant. The reader only knows what you wrote.

The second check is the adverb. I do not hate adverbs, and I will defend a good one against anyone. But I notice that my weakest sentences lean on them. She said it softly. He walked slowly. They waited quietly. In each case the verb was too timid to do its own job, so I handed it a crutch. The words only, family, early and lovely end in "ly" and are not adverbs in that sense, so a good checker lets them alone, and so should I. Likewise a reply is not an adverb, and neither is July.

The third check is a list of my own bad habits. I started to write "she felt" so often that the phrase became a tic. She felt the cold. She felt a hand on her shoulder. She felt sort of sad. I noticed the habit only because a friend circled it in red, twice, on every page, and wrote a single word in the margin: why? Since then I keep a short list on a separate note, and I read it before I send anything out. The list is not a rule. It is a memory of the mistakes I tend to repeat.

The fourth check is the long sentence, and I will be honest about it: I love a long sentence, I protect it from editors, and I still believe that a good one can carry a reader across a whole page without a single stumble, if each clause hands the reader gently to the next, and if the rhythm of the thing is steady enough that the breath does not run out before the period arrives, which it must, eventually, even if the writer had hoped it never would.

A short one is a relief after that. So is a pause.

%% beat: the writer meets the editor in the café %%

I met my editor James in a café last spring. He started to tell me about a novel he was proofing, and then he stopped and looked at the cup. "You know what the worst word in English is?" he asked. "Very." I laughed. He did not.

%% XXX: add the actual name of the café %%

He told me that every manuscript he loves has a hundred small flaws, and that his job is not to remove them but to decide which ones belong to the book. A flaw can be a voice. A repetition can be a spell. What he cannot forgive is the flaw nobody chose. That idea has stayed with me longer than any advice about style, and I think it is the real reason for the notebook, the list and the walks to the window.

Jaems, my other editor, is the opposite. He cuts everything he can reach, and then he cuts a little more. I once saw him take a paragraph of mine down to a single line, and the line was better. I felt a little betrayed, and a lot grateful, and when I carried the single line home through the rain, past the shuttered bakery and the bus stop where nobody ever waits, I understood that both feelings were fair and that neither one needed to win.

The people in these stories are friends, so their names matter to me, and I check them as carefully as I check the commas. A name spelled two ways in one note is a small betrayal of a real person. James is James, Anna is Anna, and the machine should tell me when I have typed Anne by accident, never when I write Anna's book or the Annas of the world.

I keep the checks in a file called `revision-notes.md`, and the list of my habits lives in [[Word lists|my word lists]], next to the names. None of it rewrites anything. The marks sit under the words like a quiet question, and I decide. That is the whole point: a revision tool should feel like a second pair of eyes and never like a second pair of hands.

When I read the last page again, I try to hear it as a stranger would. The wind was starting to rise, and the street outside was starting to empty, and I was running out of tea. I closed the notebook, and I heard the clock, and I felt ready to read the first paragraph a fourth time.
